content.title: What is Stack Implementation?
content.description: Stack implementation refers to the internal mechanism used to store and manage stack elements while supporting Push, Pop, Peek, and other operations efficiently.

content.content: Although the Stack follows the same LIFO principle regardless of implementation, its internal storage can vary. The two most common approaches are Array-Based Stack and Linked List-Based Stack.

content.title: Key Idea
content.content: The behavior of a Stack remains the same regardless of implementation. Only the underlying storage mechanism changes.
Why Do We Need Different Implementations?
Different applications have different memory requirements. Some systems require fixed-size storage while others need dynamic growth. This is why multiple stack implementations exist.
An Array-Based Stack stores elements inside a contiguous memory block. A variable called top keeps track of the most recently inserted element.

content.title: Top Pointer
content.description: The top variable always points to the last inserted element and helps perform Push and Pop operations efficiently.

content.title: Advantage
content.content: Array-based stacks provide excellent cache performance because elements are stored contiguously in memory.

content.title: Limitation
content.content: If the stack size is fixed, inserting beyond capacity causes Stack Overflow.
In a Linked List Stack, each element is stored inside a node containing data and a reference to the next node. The top pointer points to the first node.

content.title: Dynamic Growth
content.description: Linked list stacks grow dynamically as new nodes are created, eliminating fixed-size limitations.

Advantage
content.content: Linked List stacks can grow dynamically without worrying about predefined capacity.
Modern programming languages often use dynamic arrays internally. When the stack becomes full, a larger array is created and elements are copied.

content.title: Industry Usage
content.content: Java Stack implementations and C++ STL stacks often rely on dynamic containers internally.

items.question: Compiler Design
items.answer: Used for syntax parsing and expression evaluation.

items.question: What causes Overflow?
items.answer: Pushing into a full fixed-size array stack.

items.question: Common Linked List Error?
items.answer: Not updating the top pointer correctly.

content.title: Interview Tip
content.content: Always discuss both Array-Based and Linked List-Based implementations when asked about Stack design in interviews.

content.title: Interview Insight
content.description: Most interview questions expect you to understand the trade-offs between array and linked list implementations rather than just coding the stack.

content.title: Quick Revision
points: Stacks can be implemented using arrays or linked lists.
Push and Pop take O(1) time in both implementations.
Array stacks may overflow when capacity is exceeded.
Linked list stacks require extra memory for pointers.
Dynamic arrays help overcome fixed-size limitations.
Implementation choice depends on application requirements.
